how-to-fix-a-publicly-listable-bucket.ht.text:
← Cloud Bucket Exposure Checker

How to fix a publicly listable bucket

If Cloud Bucket Exposure Checker (or any other check) just reported that an AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage bucket allows anonymous public listing, the fix is a provider setting, not a file you delete -- and it is a different setting on each of the three. The order below closes the listing first, then checks the separate thing a clean listing result does not cover.

1. Block anonymous listing at the provider

Deleting the object you were worried about does nothing to the bucket's own listing permission -- the next anonymous request can still enumerate whatever is left. Fix the setting that actually controls it: 

# AWS S3 -- block public access at the bucket (and prefer the account-level
# setting too, so a future bucket cannot be created public by default)
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket YOUR-BUCKET \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true

# Google Cloud Storage -- turn on Public Access Prevention, and remove any
# allUsers / allAuthenticatedUsers grant from the bucket's own IAM policy
gcloud storage buckets update gs://YOUR-BUCKET --public-access-prevention
gcloud storage buckets remove-iam-policy-binding gs://YOUR-BUCKET \
  --member=allUsers --role=roles/storage.objectViewer

# Azure Blob Storage -- set the container's public access level to Private
az storage container set-permission --name YOUR-CONTAINER \
  --account-name YOUR-ACCOUNT --public-access off

A Block Public Access setting or an explicit ACL/IAM grant can each cause the same symptom on AWS and GCS -- check both a bucket policy and the legacy ACL on S3, and both Public Access Prevention and the IAM policy on GCS. Azure's per-container public access level is the one setting that governs both listing and object read together, unlike S3 and GCS, where they are separate.

2. Re-run the checker to confirm the listing itself is closed

node check.mjs <bucket-url> again, against the same URL. A private or not-found result means the one request this tool ever sends -- the anonymous LIST -- is now refused or the bucket no longer resolves. That confirms listing is fixed. It does not confirm anything about whether an individual object is still publicly readable, because this tool was never designed to test that -- see step 3.

3. Check public object-read access separately

A bucket can have listing blocked while a direct link to a known object key still resolves publicly -- a real, separate exposure this checker cannot detect, because it never has an object key to test without a listing to find one in. Confirm it with the provider's own tooling instead of assuming a clean listing result covers it: AWS IAM Access Analyzer for S3 (flags buckets and objects reachable from outside the account), the Public access badge GCS shows per bucket in the console, or Azure's container-level public access setting, which -- unlike S3 and GCS -- already controls object read at the same time as listing, so fixing step 1 on Azure fixes both.

4. Find out how it became public, and fix that too

A bucket rarely goes public by itself. The common causes are a bucket policy or ACL added for a one-off integration and never removed, an infrastructure-as-code module whose default is public-read, or a manual console change nobody recorded. Check every other bucket the same account, team, or Terraform/CloudFormation module created for the same misconfiguration -- a fix applied to one bucket at a time is exactly how the next one gets missed -- and turn on account-level Block Public Access (S3) or org-level Public Access Prevention (GCS) so a newly created bucket cannot repeat it by default.

You are responsible for verifying these steps against your own environment before relying on them, and for having authorisation to change any account, bucket, or container you act on.

Cloud Bucket Exposure Checker

Sends one real, read-only HTTP GET request -- a cloud provider's own anonymous listing endpoint -- to an AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage bucket you choose, and checks whether the response is a real, well-formed listing document, not just whether the status code is 200. A publicly listable bucket lets anyone on the internet enumerate every object name with no credentials -- and if the bucket also allows public object reads, every listed name is directly downloadable. Only point it at a bucket you own or are authorised to test.

See this checker vs. manually checking in the cloud console — the case a quick console glance misses. Already found a publicly listable bucket? How to fix it, per provider.

A clean report here only covers listing. See public listing vs. public read for why a bucket can still hand out object content even when this checker reports it private, and the exact setting that closes each on S3, GCS, and Azure.

1. Run the CLI against your bucket

Node.js, no dependencies to install:

node check.mjs https://your-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/ --json
node check.mjs --provider gcs --bucket your-bucket --json
node check.mjs --provider azure --bucket your-container --account your-storage-account --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and engine.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the bucket you name; nothing goes through this site, and it never fetches any individual object's content, only the listing.

2. Paste the JSON output here

Paste the JSON from step 1 and click Check.

Report

Raw probe result

Common questions

What can someone actually do with a publicly listable bucket?

Anyone can enumerate every object name in the bucket with no credentials at all -- and object names alone are often sensitive on their own: customer IDs, internal filenames, database backup dates, employee names in a photo path. If the same bucket is ALSO configured to allow public object reads (a separate setting this tool does not test), every listed name becomes directly downloadable. This is the mechanism behind a long list of real breaches -- Verizon (14 million customer records, 2017), a Pentagon contractor's exposed social-media-monitoring archive, and dozens of Have I Been Pwned entries -- and it is exactly why AWS now turns "Block Public Access" on by default for every new bucket. More background: why cloud buckets end up publicly listable despite that default.

Why does this only check listing, and not whether the files themselves are downloadable?

Finding out a bucket allows public listing is the exposure this tool checks; downloading what is inside it is a different, higher-liability action a real authorised penetration test would take. This tool sends exactly one request -- the listing endpoint -- and never issues a GET against any individual object key it finds, the same restraint git-exposure-check documents for not requesting a repository's packed objects once HEAD/config already confirm exposure. A bucket can also be configured so objects are publicly readable even when listing is blocked (a direct link still works); that is a real, separate exposure this tool does not detect, because it never has an object key to test without a listing to find one in.

Why does this need a CLI instead of just checking a bucket name I type into the page?

A cloud provider's bucket-listing endpoint does not send permissive CORS headers by default, so a browser tab cannot reliably read the response even though the request itself would go out -- the same CORS restriction git-exposure-check and cors-misconfig-check document for checking an arbitrary third-party endpoint from inside a page. A small local CLI with no such restriction, run from your own machine, gets a definitive answer every time.

Does a clean report mean my bucket has no exposure at all?

No. This checks one specific, well-documented exposure class -- anonymous public LISTING at the one bucket or container you point it at. It does not check public object-read access, bucket policies for authenticated-but-not-owner roles, object ACLs on individual files, server-side encryption, versioning, or logging, and it only checks the one bucket you name, not every bucket in an account. Treat a clean report as evidence about this one exposure class on this one bucket, not a full cloud security assessment.

Why only AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob Storage?

Those three are the object-storage services most commonly left publicly listable by an accidental misconfiguration, and each publishes a stable, documented anonymous-listing response shape this tool can classify without guessing: AWS S3 and Google Cloud Storage share an S3-compatible XML API (a ListBucketResult root element), and Azure Blob Storage has its own EnumerationResults schema. A provider without a documented anonymous-listing endpoint in this same request-response shape is out of scope rather than guessed at.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks one specific, well-documented exposure class -- anonymous public listing at the one bucket or container you give it. It does not check public object-read access, authenticated-role policies, object ACLs, encryption, versioning, or logging, and cannot see a pattern it doesn't check for. A clean report describes what this one request found, not a guarantee the bucket has no exposure.

public-listing-vs-public-read.html.text:
← Back to the Cloud Bucket Exposure Checker

Public listing vs. public read: why fixing one doesn't fix the other

"Is this bucket exposed?" is really two independent questions on every major cloud storage provider: can a stranger enumerate what's inside it with no credentials (listing), and can a stranger download a file whose name they already know or guessed (read)? A provider can be configured to allow either alone, both, or neither. This tool checks listing only -- the request it sends is each provider's own bucket-listing endpoint, never a GET on an individual object. A clean "private" or "not-found" result here says nothing about whether a known object key is still downloadable.

AWS S3: two separate IAM actions

A bucket policy statement (or a legacy ACL grant) names a specific action. s3:ListBucket controls anonymous listing; s3:GetObject controls anonymous reads of individual keys. A policy can grant one without the other. Block Public Access has its own split: BlockPublicPolicy stops a new public policy statement from taking effect, while RestrictPublicBuckets stops an existing public policy from applying, at the bucket or account level. Removing a wildcard s3:ListBucket statement does nothing to a separate s3:GetObject grant sitting in the same document, or in an old ACL nobody has looked at since.

Google Cloud Storage: a role can bundle both, or neither

roles/storage.objectViewer grants both storage.objects.get (read) and storage.objects.list (listing) together, so binding it to allUsers opens both at once. A narrower custom role can grant just one of the two permissions, and older projects sometimes carry exactly that. Bucket-level Public Access Prevention (or the equivalent organization policy) blocks any public IAM binding outright -- the one GCS setting that closes both at the same time. Reading the console's permissions list one binding at a time, and stopping at the first one you remove, can leave the other in place.

Azure Blob Storage: the setting names the split explicitly

A container's Public access level is one of three values:

SettingAnonymous listingAnonymous read of a known blob URL
PrivateNoNo
BlobNoYes
ContainerYesYes

Setting Blob instead of Private for a container that needs public downloads is a common, deliberate choice — and it means this checker's own probe (which calls the listing endpoint, ?restype=container&comp=list) reports private for a container that is still handing out every object's content to anyone who has, or guesses, its URL. The account-level Allow Blob public access switch sits above the container setting: disabling it blocks both Blob and Container levels account-wide in one move, which is the one Azure setting that closes both at once.

What this checker's verdict actually tells you

This tool sends exactly one request, the listing endpoint, and classifies the response body: a real ListBucketResult or EnumerationResults document means public listing; an error body carrying a code like AccessDenied, PublicAccessNotPermitted, or AuthorizationPermissionMismatch means the provider denied the anonymous listing request. Either result is real evidence about listing — and neither one is evidence about read. If you need to know whether a specific object is downloadable, that is a separate request against that object's own URL, checked against a key you already know rather than one this tool's listing just handed you.

Run the Cloud Bucket Exposure Checker against your own bucket or container to see today's listing verdict. Only run it against a target you own or are authorised to test.

vs-manually-checking-in-the-cloud-consol.text:
Cloud Bucket Exposure Checker vs. Manually Checking in the Cloud Console

Names no specific company or product — this compares against clicking through your own provider's console, a manual habit every bucket owner already has, not a company or product this could be mistaken for.

Checking the console by handThis tool
What it readsThe settings a person configured — bucket policy, ACLs, the account-level public-access toggleThe actual response an anonymous, unauthenticated request receives
Catches a policy/ACL/account-toggle conflictOnly if you know which layer wins and check the right oneYes — it sends the real request, so it reports what wins, not what any one setting says in isolation
Repeatable in CINo — a manual click-throughYes — a scriptable exit code (0 private/not-found, 1 exposed)
Catches drift after a deploy or a policy editOnly the next time someone happens to lookEvery run, on demand or on a schedule

What does checking the console by hand actually show you?

Your cloud provider's console shows you the settings you (or someone on your team) configured: a bucket policy document, an ACL grant list, an account-level "Block Public Access" toggle. That is a real, useful read of intent -- what the configuration says should happen.

Where does the by-hand check fall short?

Several independent settings can each grant or block public listing, and the console shows each one separately -- it does not always make obvious which one actually wins for an anonymous, unauthenticated request. A bucket policy statement can grant s3:ListBucket to a wildcard principal while a different admin reads only the account-level Block Public Access toggle and sees it enabled, not realising a resource-level policy can still take effect depending on how it was applied. An old ACL grant from before a stricter policy was added can persist unnoticed. A storage account's container-level "Public access level" in Azure can be set independently of the account's own "Allow Blob public access" setting, and either alone reading "restricted" does not confirm the other agrees. The only way to know for certain what an anonymous outsider receives is to actually send the anonymous request they would send -- which is what this tool does, and reading five separate settings correctly by hand does not replace.

Why does this matter for CI, not just a one-time check?

A console check is a point-in-time, manual look. A new bucket policy statement, a fresh IaC deploy, or a teammate widening an ACL for a one-off debugging session can reopen a bucket at any point after the last time someone happened to look. The CLI here returns a real exit code, so it can gate a deploy the same way a linter or test suite does -- catching a regression the day it ships rather than the next time someone thinks to open the console.

← Back to the checker

Evidence, not a determination. This checks one specific, well-documented exposure class — anonymous public listing at the one bucket or container you give it. A clean report describes what one request found, not a guarantee the bucket has no exposure.

why-do-cloud-buckets-end-up-publicly-lis.text:
← Cloud bucket exposure checker

Why do cloud buckets end up publicly listable?

Every major provider defaults a newly created bucket or container to private, and AWS has gone further than a default: since 2018 it offers Block Public Access, an account-level switch that overrides any bucket policy or ACL underneath it and can only be turned off deliberately. Despite that, publicly listable buckets keep turning up in security research and breach disclosures years later -- including the two cited on this checker's own page: 14 million Verizon customer records exposed through a vendor's misconfigured S3 bucket in 2017, and a Pentagon contractor's exposed monitoring archive the same year. The defaults are not the problem; what overrides them is.

Three separate settings, and any one of them can win

A bucket's effective access is not one switch, it's several, layered:

LayerWhat it isHow it goes wrong
ACL (S3, legacy)A per-object or per-bucket grant list, older than bucket policiesA grant to the AllUsers group made years ago, before Block Public Access existed, quietly persists
Bucket policy (S3, GCS IAM)A JSON document naming who can do whatA statement written for a static-website-hosting tutorial grants s3:GetObject to Principal: "*" -- and a later edit, meant to widen read access for one prefix, is copy-pasted without scoping the Resource field, granting s3:ListBucket too
Account/container-level toggleAWS's account-wide Block Public Access; Azure's per-account "Allow Blob public access" plus a separate per-container public-access levelTwo independent settings that both have to agree "private" -- an admin who checks only one assumes the other matches

Any layer that permits the request wins for an actual anonymous visitor, regardless of what the other layers say -- which is exactly why reading each setting in the console is a different question from sending the real request and seeing what comes back.

The recurring path: infrastructure meant to be public, scoped too wide

The single most common route to an exposed bucket is not an admin deliberately choosing "public" for private data -- it's a bucket that was supposed to allow some public access (a static website, a public dataset, a CDN origin, a CI artifact download) getting a policy or ACL broad enough to also permit listing every other object inside it. A policy statement written to let anyone GetObject a website's HTML and images does not need ListBucket at all -- but templates copied from tutorials, and IaC modules reused across projects, often grant both together because nobody removed the unneeded permission before applying it to a bucket that also holds internal files.

Forgotten buckets compound it: a staging or migration bucket created for a one-time job, given a wide-open policy to make the job easier, and never revisited once the job finished. Nothing about a bucket's public-listing state changes on its own after that -- it stays exactly as wide as the last edit left it until someone checks again.

Check your own bucket

A free tool that runs exactly the check above -- one real, read-only request to a bucket or container's own anonymous listing endpoint across AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage -- is at the cloud bucket exposure checker. It never fetches any object's own content, only the listing, and it sends nothing about the bucket or the result to this site. As with any tool that sends requests to infrastructure you name, only run it against a bucket or container you own or are authorised to test.
